issues.detail: Overly long, tutorial-style scenario for a single conceptual Maillard vs caramelization distinction; calibration items are much more concise and direct.
Prompt embeds meta-interpretation of the phrase 'oxidizing sugars' and explanation of redox roles; source items state the fact more simply.
HLB-number reasoning and matching to specific products is more advanced than typical Div B 2022 items and may be closer to Div C depth.
Mixes process-survival and pre-formed toxin in one stem; options are not parallel and the stem over-explains pasteurization design.
Essentially a trivial ratio comparison framed in words; similar numeric-comparison skills are already exercised elsewhere in the bank.
Hydrometer/density setup is generic physical-science reasoning with minimal food-specific content; calibration corpus tends to keep questions tightly tied to food chemistry or nutrition.
Four-condition pineapple–gelatin setup is more verbose than needed for the classic bromelain-denaturation concept tested in Div B.
Botulism control in garlic-in-oil with specific pH and aw values is more like upper-level food microbiology/HACCP than typical Div B 2022 expectations.
Part (b) depends on (a) only superficially (simple percent), and (c) is conceptually independent; the shared scenario does not create strong multi-step depth beyond basic arithmetic plus recall.
Multiple parts (a, c, d) all ask for experimental-design interpretation around the same Maillard dataset; this is denser and more repetitive than single-part calibration questions.
Combined interpretation, percent-change calculation, control justification, and variable-control reasoning in one 7-point item is more complex than typical Div B 2022 style.
Abstract aw–pH growth-limit modeling with multiple organisms and a hurdle-technology explanation is closer to advanced food micro; calibration examples do not go this deep on preservation modeling.
Parts (a), (b), and (d) all require similar inequality checks against the same aw/pH thresholds, leading to repetitive logic.
Part (e) asks for designing a denaturation vs reversible-temperature-effect experiment, which is more sophisticated than the short factual or simple-design prompts in the calibration set.

Several parts are loosely connected (basic variable ID, percent increase, choice of temperature, mechanism explanation, then a new design task), making the item feel like a mini-lab writeup rather than a single focused question as in the source corpus.

Compared to source topic counts, the bank underrepresents analytical_tests and experimental_analysis as standalone foci and overweights multi-part experimental FRQs, diverging from the mostly single-question calibration style.
Generated set has relatively more difficulty 3–4 multi-step reasoning items than the source, which is dominated by short, single-step questions even at difficulty 4.
Many stems are written in a narrative, classroom-activity tone with extended context and explicit modeling language, whereas calibration items are terse, test-like prompts with minimal scenario text.
